utterances.text: The entire population of Osmace fled to Subin. We had quite a few wounded, women and children. And the shelling started from Brezani and shells were hitting the school where quite a few people had taken shelter. Ibrahim Malagic's family was killed on that occasion, and then the wife of Ismet Malagic and his three children were injured, and Alija Delic's son was killed as well. And so that shelling came from Brezani, so that's to the west of Osmace. And then we abandoned the village and withdrew to Subin through the woods, and I myself was in that group of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. For our purposes we are interested in among other things damage which could be caused to property by shelling. Did you return to Osmace and did you see the effect of the shelling which you've described?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: In the evening hours, we went back to the village, and there are two hamlets, Mahala and Hetavica [phoen] which are on the hill, and they had been totally devastated. There wasn't a single house left undamaged, at least the windows or the roof or whatever, everything was damaged and destroyed. Whatever could be destroyed was destroyed in that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the effect obviously of Serb shelling over, what, a three-hour period, I think you've said?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Roughly speaking three hours. That's what I suppose. And Serbs didn't have the courage, and I don't know for what reason, but anyway, they didn't have the courage to enter with the infantry into the village, although the village had been totally surrounded, perhaps they thought that people might have been armed, or I don't know for what reason but at any rate they withdrew in the afternoon and that's when the exodus started. Whatever was not torched on the 7th of May, that is to say Jezero, Posevar, Hadzici, Trubari, Dobrak, et cetera, was finished off on the 8th of May. So whatever they failed it destroy on the 7th of May was finished off on the 8th of May, and razed to the ground. And let me just add that Osmace had about 300 houses with all the sheds, et cetera, and so 99 per cent of that property was totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Just on that theme, did you continue to live in these damaged and destroyed houses in the months that followed?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. People made do as best they could. They would have a plastic sheeting, in lieu of a roof, of one room, or they could take some building materials from the sheds and stables so as to be able to make those houses habitable. And if I may continue, on that same day, on the 8th of May, that is, on the other side of the river, Serbs torched all villages, Voljavica, Zaluze, Tegare, from the direction of Bratunac. That was on the 8th of May. And we are talking about 2.000 to 3.000 houses that were torched on that day and that entire population was forced to withdraw in the direction of Mocevici, Poznanovici, and those villages higher up to the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any of those refugees in your village, from those areas, Zanjevo, Voljavica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: As I stated a minute ago, the entire population of the area went to Osmace to the -- that is the area of Mihoilavici [phoen] and Delici, and that the refugees outnumbered the local populace by two or three times. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please I have no problems with the answers just given. It's line 14, down. The witness said the infantry didn't enter Osmace although it was surrounded and I understood that he said it was shelled, and then referred to withdrawal in the afternoon and it's not clear to me what he's talking about, whether they withdrew from the centre of Osmace or not. And then the witness went on to say that whatever they failed to destroy on the 7th was finished off on the 8th and razed to the ground. Now, I think in order for you to understand this evidence of destruction you must know whether it was razed by arson, torching, and so on, or whether the witness is talking about destruction by shelling. So it's that one answer that is just not clear to me. I don't know if the Serb troops went into the village one day or both days or how the damage was caused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's right. I'll leave that in the hands of Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify this Mr. Buric, and if you could just be yes or no if possible so we can clarify it simply. First of all did the Serbs actually enter Osmace, the village of Osmace, on the day that you've been speaking about?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you described the Serbs withdrawing or if that's the term, where were they withdrawing from and where were they withdrawing to?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I already stated that in the morning, three buses of Serb soldiers arrived and that they surrounded the village of Osmace and they were firing at the population that was fleeing the village. They were not entering the village itself. They were firing at the civilians fleeing towards the woods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that all the damage that you saw in Osmace was done by shelling rather than by arson?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, when you said whatever was not burnt that day or whatever hadn't been burnt before they then burnt -- what areas were you referring Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to where other villages or houses were razed?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: As I said, that when their units were withdrawing, they were torching the Muslim villages or whatever was left since the 7th, either houses or the outhouses. So they finished it off. That was in Trubari, Jezero and Posevar, Dobrak, Vesovici [phoen], Skelani, Lijesce, Mala and Velika Daljegosta, and up the Drina, Zanjo [phoen], Voljavica, Tegare. That was all on the 7th and the 8th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, the Serbs didn't go into Osmace and burn houses, they shelled Osmace. As they withdrew they then went and burnt what had already not been destroyed in the Muslim villages which you just mentioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, just dealing with the Muslim villages along the Drina, Voljavica, Abdulici, Zanjevo, do you know what happened to the possessions of those Muslims who had to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: All possessions belonging to the Muslims who fled from their villages was taken and then the houses and outhouses were torched, as well as whatever it was that they couldn't take with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd ask if the witness could be shown the next exhibit which is ERN number 04360191. And it reads at the top, "Minutes, the minutes prepared by the military police and Vukoman Simic on handover of objects confiscated from citizens from the area of Fakovici that were collected from Muslim houses and facilities as follows." And it refers to a list follows of various items. Now, firstly, if you can just help us with this: Looking at the names, Vukoman Simic, Miodrag Cvetkovic, Radenko Milesic, are these Serb or Muslim names?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I believe these were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So then this is minutes prepared by Serb military police reporting on goods confiscated from Fakovici, which -- goods which had been collected from Muslim houses and facilities. If you can cast your eye down the list are you familiar with deserted Muslim houses being pillaged of doors and windows and other items mentioned there by the Serbs??

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Not only these things but the Serbs took anything that was of value. Whatever they found in the Muslim villages from -- including agricultural machinery, trucks, food. This is just a scratch on the surface of everything they took.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you did get in 1 per cent -- one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Not even .1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 0.1 per cent, that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will become, Mr. Jones, Defence Exhibit D739.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, going to play a video exhibit in a moment. It's D177. And just by way of background, you've referred to how Muslim villages were burnt, torched, Muslims were killed in the Skelani area in May 1992. Do you know, and perhaps you've told us, but where all these Muslims went when their homes were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: The Muslims from the Podrinje villages were fleeing into the woods, most of them, and they left towards Osmace, Tokoljak, Miholjevine, Delici, and Poznanovici on the other side as well as Mocevici, Dimnici, Storeska, Karacici, the Osatik [phoen] region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to play this video which -- it lasts 13 minutes. It's a Defence Exhibit. We have transcripts already. I'm going to ask you, Mr. Buric, to comment as we go along, if you recognise any of the places or the people or if you feel you can add useful information, then please just do so and we'll pause the video at that moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Perhaps before we begin, I omitted to say something. Since the houses had already been damaged by shelling in the Muslim villages, a lot of the population was moving about together in groups, and they used makeshift shelter, they dug out holes that they would cover in the woods, so one could find entire settlements in Biljeg on Tokoljacko Brdo and Sehiti, containing several hundred people in shacks. They used anything they could find, local vegetation, without the minimum ability to live and survive there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you go to any of those places you mentioned, any of those camps?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were large groups of people. I wouldn't call it camp or settlement but simply groups, a place of refuge. One of them was in a forest and the other one was on Tokoljacko Brdo, where people from Radovcici, Juscici [phoen], and Katanici, and Tokoljaci were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll play the video.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this woman's name was Nesiba Smajic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we also saw reference to Sehiti camp a moment ago which I take is the one, the Sehiti you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes, Sehiti.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zildzija Smajic. That was the man with the beard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, I am not commenting anything for the record because I find it difficult to do so because you've got the date which is not even -- not even clearly established, and then an hour and a minute, which hasn't changed as yet. So I wouldn't -- I wouldn't know which fragment of the video to refer when he is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I see what Your Honour means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the problem that I have. MR. JONES: That way we're satisfied that he's identifying people as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If we have difficulties on this, of course, we can always see the transcript, see the video recording of the sitting. I wanted to confirm to you why I am not commenting myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, I suppose the only other way to do with it would be to refer to when the subtitles appear, but I think that would be too lengthy. So I think it's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you have any other suggestion, please come forward but I have been thinking about how to approach it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I haven't got a solution myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In fact it's being pointed out by our CaseMap manager that there is -- there are numbers at the bottom, 0213.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is it? Let me see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In small, green numbers. Bottom right-hand corner, at least on our version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Oh, I see, I see, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I can read that out if it helps. I have it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nezir Smajic is the man with the -- for -- falling on the -- 11.48.15 over the eye, and this is Nezir's Smajic's son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, we are at 03 minutes point 32 seconds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where they are from?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. From the village of Tokoljak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was burnt on the 8th of May; is that correct, 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the villages that was torched in May, Trubari, Radovcici, Ivcici, Katanici, and Tokoljaci. So all of these people were at this place of refuge in May in Sehiti and Tokoljacko Brdo. There were two separate locations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We've heard at the beginning of the video that it's August 1992, and mentioned that there were -- the villages burnt three months before, which brings us to May. I just make that observation. Thank you, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Dzevada Dzananovic, the woman who came out of the shack. She used to be a teacher. And her brother was a physician.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which village was she from?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: From Tokoljaca [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, the comments by the witness were made when we had arrived at still 06 minutes 18 seconds. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Akif Smajic, the boy talking now, from Tokoljaci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are now at, for the record, at 07 minutes, point 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The man in the white shirt is Hamzo Smajic from Tokoljaci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for the record we are now at 07 minutes, 42 seconds. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a question at this point. We see on the screen that the refugee you just identified is saying, "We were receiving refugees that came from all sides." Now, would you interpret that to mean that Serbs, Muslims and perhaps Croats were all living in the woods in interethnic harmony at this time or would you interpret it in some other way?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No. He was talking about the torching of Muslim villages from various parts of the region. They had in mind Zanjevo, which is towards the north of the region, Tokoljaci and Radovcici was to the east. So we are talking only about Muslims from various villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, at this time, this is August 1992 - sorry, if I can just put the question - were you aware of any Serb refugees in the Skelani area living in the woods under nylons, without food, without shelter?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We'll carry on with the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, since we missed the first two comments by the witness, do you want us to go back to the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, that's not necessary, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you one thing which relates to an answer you gave before we looked at the video. You referred to Biljeg area. And if you'll give me a moment I'll just find what you said. It's line -- page 51, line 12. You refer to entire settlements in Biljeg. Were those settlements anything like those which we've seen in the video? And I'm talking about the period May to August 1992.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was always the same. We are talking about the Muslim population which fled to the woods, in totally inhumane conditions. There wasn't a minimum of hygiene for those people. They had diseases such as scabies. They were flea bitten and they didn't have any water, and I was in a settlement called Sehiti where there is a source of water. That's where the water supply for my village of Osmace comes from, and together with a couple of other lads from my village, we went there and we told them that they could use that source of water in order for them to have some drinking water, because we had about 300 people there, and we got a hose for them because we had another possibility to get water in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I just want to focus on Biljeg for a moment because we saw an exhibit a moment ago, P4, in which there is a reference to a Biljeg Territorial Defence to be organised and a suggestion perhaps that there was a self-organised armed group in Biljeg. And that's in June 1992. I want -- would you agree or disagree that in these conditions that you've described in Biljeg, there was an organised, armed group on its way to becoming a well-organised Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No. There were no units or organised groups of any kind. There were locals from Miholjevine, Delici [phoen], Mocici there, and people who had fled. I mean, those people who didn't want to go to Macedonia and so from Jagosta [phoen] and Skelani they joined this group of people who were hiding in the woods in Miholjevine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And to put this in a time frame, when -- what period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: May, beginning of June, the end of May, the beginning of June. And there were no organised armed units in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to probe that a bit more in relation to Osmace. I'm going to ask you a series of questions and if you can just answer yes or no, if possible, did you have in Osmace in this period, May/June 1992, did you have a commander who would issue orders to the fighters in Osmace?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have ranks?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have barracks?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an armoury?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you paid salaries, those of you who were fighters?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any way of making someone do something he didn't want to do, a fighter, let's say, to go to fight when he preferred to stay at home?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No. Everything was absolutely voluntary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if someone were to say and --.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, my reference is to something in the official transcript of the hearing of 8th of June 2005, page 9013.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If someone were to say that as early as April 1992, that Muslim forces operating in the Srebrenica area operated in organised structure, would that, by any stretch of the imagination, be true?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: That would be 100 per cent incorrect. Not even in March 1993 did we have any organised units in that way. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, are we to read that answer as applying "100 per cent incorrect, not even in March, 1993," does that apply to the entire Srebrenica area or could we at least get some idea, just make sure that the witness is not talking just about Osmace but the wider area? That's the way I understood it but it's not absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understood it, too, but, of course, Mr. Jones, please. You can put a direct question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me put it this way: In Osmace, your fighters in Osmace, up until March 1993, did you operate as part of an organised structure in the area of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: There was no structure whatsoever in March, April, May, and the year I'm referring to here is 1992. And I'm talking about the situation within the village, but I can also refer to the broader area with regard to March 1993. So in March 1993, when most villages had fallen, the entire area had fallen, then there was no sort of structure whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I'm going to come to March 1993 in a moment, but still -- while I still have the same reference to the transcript, if someone were to say that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, again as early as April 1992, had structures, command and control arrangements in, and we'll limit it to your area, let's say Osmace, would that be true to your knowledge that your fighters in Osmace were part of an ABiH command and control structure?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I can state with a great deal of responsibility that never, ever, had there been an organised structure of military units at Osmace. Never, ever. We had 21 rifles, about 50 lads who had no logistics, no arms, no ammunition supplies, nothing at all which could be qualified as a military. People slept in their own houses. There was no specific place where they could gather together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask if the witness could be shown Prosecution Exhibit P80, please. Now, this is obviously a lengthy document. Did you see this document with me when you came to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't recall us reviewing this document in our offices in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Well, in that case, take your time to peruse this document. For the record it's dated 19 September 1993 but it's referring back to the period from April 1992 onwards and it's purportedly describing the formation, structure of the Srebrenica armed forces during the past period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's confirm first of all that he's got the right document in front of him, Mr. Jones, to make sure, since he's not remembering having seen this document before. Usher, please, can you put the first page of this document that the witness is reading now on the ELMO so that I can confirm which document he is reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It is. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please hand it back to the witness, and Mr. Jones you may proceed with your questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it's a lengthy document but I only need to take to you the parts relating to Osmace and Kragljivoda. So I'll take you directly to those parts. Firstly, you see on the first page it deals with the first formation structure and it's dealing with the time period from 17th April 1992 to mid-October 1992. And if we go to number 3, which I think it's on the first page still of the B/C/S but page 2 of the English, it says "TO Osmace." Do you see that? "TO Osmace, Ceta, Tokoljaci Ceta, Osmace, Poznanovici." Do you see that, Mr. Buric?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Simply a couple of questions. In this period, to your -- April 1992 to October 1992, to your knowledge, was there something which could be described as a TO Osmace consisting of three companies, a Tokoljaci company, an Osmace company and a Poznanovici company? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Never. We never had anything of the sort, and we never had any link to Tokoljaci or Poznanovici and there was no Osmace company as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's wrong. Did you have conscripts, i.e., people who were conscripted into service as opposed to joining voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So that too is wrong. Did you have 121 fighters in Osmace in -- in Osmace?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: In March 1993, we didn't have that number of fighters. That was at the end of war. And the period that you're referring to, certainly not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that too is false. Let's look at TO Kragljivoda. Were there conscripts in Kragljivoda, so far as you're aware, i.e., people who were conscripted into military service?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I really never, ever heard anything about the area of Srebrenica, the region of Srebrenica, having had any place where even a dozen lads could go through some kind of training. This is the first I've heard of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Sefik Mandzic, to your knowledge, have, as this document suggests, 235 conscripts under his command between April and October 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I believe that the region around Kalina didn't have 235 inhabitants, let alone soldiers. I'm just talking to you about the population. Had they had so many soldiers, no, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many fighters do you think -- well, rather, do you think -- do you know where in Kragljivoda in that period, April to October 1992, roughly?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I think that there could have been about 50 lads tops, with Sefik, within that group. And as to that particular position, never more than 10 or 15 at Kragljivoda.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. 50 maximum, 10 or 15 Kragljivoda, not 235?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It says that --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It also says, this document, that Nedzad Bektic was the commander of TO Kragljivoda, and it suggests that he was a commander over Sefik Mandzic. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No, never. Let me reiterate this. Nedzad Bektic was never a commander in Kragljivoda. The resistance organiser at Kragljivoda was Sefik Mandzic, up until his death, and then he was followed by Ibro Dudic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I won't pursue any further the inaccuracies which you've already identified for the first formation structure but I'm going to go to what's called the second formation structure which starts on page 3. And this is dealing allegedly with a position from September 1992, 3rd of September 1992. It's page 3 in English, and in B/C/S it's on the bottom of page 2. [B/C/S spoken] Do you see that? The bottom paragraph on page 2, under the heading 2.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at Osmace, what's said about Osmace and Kragljivoda. In English it's page 6, number 7, there is reference to the Independent Osmace Battalion based in Osmace. Did you have a battalion in Osmace in late 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No. As I said, in 1993 there could have been 50 armed inhabitants of Osmace at most.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would you understand to be a battalion strength unit? How many soldiers, in other words, in a battalion?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: There should be a minimum of between 300 and 600 soldiers, fully armed, with heavy machine-guns, mortars, automatic rifles, semi-automatic rifles. They had all that, the Serb side, I mean. They had a command structure, they had weapons, they had everything, and if you have a group of people with 20 hunting rifles, they can't really be called a battalion. If you think they can, well, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Esad Dudic ever any type of commander in Osmace?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Definitely. Dudic, Esad, never even had as many as ten people in his group, inhabitants, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. My question was this document says he was the acting commander of the Independent Osmace Battalion. Is that accurate, as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I know that he did not even have ten people around him and he certainly wasn't commander to anyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was Ejub Delic commander to anyone, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: He had -- no. He had about ten men, and he was from the village of Hadrovici which is a part of Osmace, and he had about ten lads with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. You say he had ten lads with him. Could he order those lads to do what he wanted? Could he issue orders, in other words?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And finally, in Kragljivoda, and I'm looking at item 3, the 3rd of May, Kragljivoda Brigade, where it says there were 927 conscripts in three battalions, can you comment on the accuracy or inaccuracy of that, what's written there?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: That's 100 per cent incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I were to describe this document as a fantasy or a work of fiction, would that be -- would that be overstating it or would you agree with that characterisation?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: This is pure fantasy. Obviously, it could have been wish thinking -- wishful thinking, I mean, on our part but this is not even 1 per cent correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify this. Had we had all this on the ground, we would have been overjoyed. But we didn't even have 1 per cent of all this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, this document, and others we've seen refers to some areas besides Kragljivoda and Osmace, namely Biljeg, Poznanovici, Tibici [phoen], Skenderovici, and I'd like, with the aid of the map, to go through these areas and if you can indicate for each of them, if you haven't already done so, the area. I'll go through one by one, and whether you had any contacts in April to June of 1992 with those areas, so let's start with Kragljivoda. In order to save time, I think I can say that you've marked Kragljivoda on the map. You've also told us of the road between Osmace and Kragljivoda and that that meant that you didn't have constant contacts or contacts indeed with Kragljivoda. If you could just answer this: What sort of contacts did you have with Kragljivoda, you in Osmace in April to June of 1992? Were they regular? Were they sporadic? Were they interrupted?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Since there was no road to speak of between Osmace and Kragljivoda, as well as all the other Muslim villages, in other words, most villages in that area of Podrinje were basically enclaves and they were isolated so in May and the beginning of June there was no contact whatsoever because there were Serb patrols all over the place. They kept coming to Kragljivoda all the time. And from the left side they came below Osmace, and on the other side they came from Brezani so we were totally isolated. So that was within the villages, people had those village guards around their houses, and they couldn't venture out seven or eight kilometres. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just before I move on, when you said that these were enclaves, would you apply that also to Biljeg?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. All Muslim villages. 99 per cent of villages in that area had no contact amongst themselves. And that includes Biljeg. They didn't have links with Poznanovici or Osmace, between Biljeg and Osmace you have a distance of about 10 kilometres and there was no contact whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then how about Mocevici? Did you have contacts with Mocevici in April to June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. Mocevici is all the way up north, and there was Brezani and Pribicevac and Spat between us. I mean, the Serb villages. And so there was no possibility of movement and there was no possibility of conveying any information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: The witness has actually just now partially answered what was the query in my mind. The witness is talking about contacts and links. He says there is none. Do I understand -- do we -- should we understand the witness to say that there was no regular communication going on or no form of communication going on, or that it was simply impossible to communicate? There is a distinction. I know it's fine but I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you like to put that to the witness, Mr. Jones, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I think I'd prefer to approach it in a different direction which is to establish what was breaking -- what was preventing communication or contacts because I think that will answer the question. It's obviously difficult for this witness to speak about all and any contacts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can deal with it in that manner. Yes, go ahead, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's deal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break shortly. I mean regulate yourself and tell me when you would like to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Since there will be an extended period with the map, this might be a good moment to ... Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. How are you going with your time estimates, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think I'm actually about on schedule for finishing tomorrow, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a 25-minute break. I think that's safer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Buric, before the break, we were exploring the problems with communications between the enclaves, the Muslim enclaves, Biljeg, Kragljivoda, Osmace, Poznanovici. You had testified that there were no contacts whatsoever between these -- between these enclaves. I want to explore in detail precisely what if any contacts there were. May I take it that you're not excluding -- and tell me if you are excluding the possibility that occasionally a person or a few people would actually manage to voyage let's say from Mocevici to Osmace or are you saying that there was absolutely no contact whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Refugees from the Drina valley managed to reach some Muslim villages via certain roads. We cannot exclude completely the possibility of some sort of contact between Osmace, Gladovici, and so on and so forth, but on the low scale, concerning any sort of organised attempts, there were none.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I want to explore first generally the sorts of things which made contacts difficult. And I'm going to deal with the period of time up to June 1992. Now, you've already mentioned in your testimony some general items or general matters which might prevent contacts. You mentioned Serb patrols on the road between Osmace and Kragljivoda. So I take it that that is something which could disrupt contacts, Serb patrols on a road. Is that something you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Serb patrols from Serb villages moved about non-stop and this is predominantly a wooded area and they sometimes went alone and it is worse to meet a single armed person than a hundred civilians. The Serb patrols patrolled around Zeleni Jadar. They would go to Brezani to Kalina, from Kalina to Toplica, from there to Postolje. There was no such communication between the Muslims because they couldn't move about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So on the one hand, we have specific Serb patrols on this road between Srebrenica and Skelani. Is it also right that there were infantry patrols, Serb infantry patrols, which was disrupting communications between enclaves? Is that -- is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. For example, from Postolje and Podrid and Toplica, where they would go -- they would go from those places to the training centre at Jezero. They would go on foot every morning and as well from Brezani on the other side from Osmace. The Serbs communicated between Brezani, Ratkovici, Ducici, and Fakovici, and it cut between the Muslim villages that were on the way. On the western side, there was Podravanje. And there was the area where the Muslim population was unable to move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I think that this is a topic of some importance to the Prosecution and we would object to questions that are leading. The previous two questions have suggested the answer, lock, stock, and barrel to the witness, and all he had to do was say "yes" and that would have been the end of it. So it's a topic of controversy and we need to be absolutely clear that what's coming out of the witness is his own evidence is and nothing that's been suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I saw you getting a little bit agitated when Mr. Jones put the question but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I respectfully disagree, Your Honour? The question amounts -- the patrols, it's just really a matter of common sense and proceeding expeditiously. The witness has said Serb patrols from Serb villages moved about non-stop and this is predominantly in a wooded area and they sometimes went alone and it's worse to meet a single armed person than a hundred civilians. It's pretty obvious that the witness is talking about Serb military patrols, so for me simply to pick up on that and say, right, Serb military controls, is not leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's finish. That question has been answered and there was no objection. That's why I allowed it in the first place, irrespective of whether it was leading or not but you've now been put on notice that on this matter, the Prosecution would object to leading questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay that's fine, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's -- and for the record, I mean, the -- please do remember that the understanding that there is between the Trial Chamber and the parties, that we will not intervene when we even -- when we consider that there is a leading question unless there is an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, explain for us, Mr. Buric, and it may be -- it may seem obvious, but why would -- why would it present a problem for communication for Muslims to communicate between each other that there are Serb villages in the vicinity? Why would that pose any problem? And this is -- I'm talking about June 1992.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: The whole of April, May, and June, there was no communication between Muslim villages, because there were Serb patrols between all of the villages. As I said a minute ago, they could move about freely. They were armed, and they turned those villages into enclaves, the villages such as Osmace, Bladojvici [phoen], Sljivica [phoen], Karacici, Ljeskovik, and on the other side, Miholjevine, Delici, Poznanovici, Podkorjen, Mocevici, between all of those villages there would be a one or a couple of Serb villages. And even physically speaking, looking at the map, it was a hindrance between the two, for example, and there was constant transportation of weaponry between their villages as well. Therefore, Muslims couldn't move around all the way until the end of June. Before that, there were no links between villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now aside from these patrols, was there anything else which presented a difficulty for Muslims to move around in the villages in this area in June 1992? Any other hazards?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. The villages were heavily shelled from all Serb positions, from Jezero, Pusici [phoen], from the Tara plateau, and on the other side from Brezani and Ratkovici. And as I said already, they used routes and forests to transport arms on horseback. And on several occasions, villagers came across such a transport and they were killed by the Serbs, when they would meet them transporting weapons in Kardinmedje [phoen] or some other Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- I'm purely summarising, you referred to patrols. You've referred to artillery. You've referred in your testimony to Sefik Mandzic. Can you remind us of how he died? Not the whole -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: The two of us helped -- went to help in Jagodnja because the Serbs from Fakovici came in and torched a part of that village in Josava.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant to interrupt you earlier but my microphone was not working. Simply without telling the story which we'll come to, what caused his death?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we -- I know where you are so why don't you put a direct question whether landmines --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- constituted also an impediment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was worried that might be leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will get there in any case, so why not get there straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the question, Mr. Buric, did landmines also pose an impediment?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Around most of their villages, Serbs laid mines, and in places where they were short of people, and where the distance between one and the other Serb village was too great, they would mine such an area, and each village was mined in itself. So Sefik Mandzic stepped on a mine on the 5th of October, together with four friends of his who tried to pull him out. They were killed the same day. Not by the same mine, of course, but the entire area was mined. The entire area around the Muslim villages that were adjacent to some Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we've referred to Biljeg before. Would you be able to mark Biljeg on the map, the area which corresponds to Biljeg?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Biljeg is not marked on the map. This is an elevation point in a wooded area. This is not a residential area. Above Mosici I believe where it says 669, I believe that to be Biljeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, you've marked that with a B?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think for the transcript I said you said Mosici rather than Mocevici. If you could spell that village you just referred to.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Mosici, M-O-S-I-C-I.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, now in June 1992, which -- what if anything stood in the way of contacts between Osmace and Biljeg? I'm speaking of specific locations rather than general problems.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Communication between Biljeg and Osmace, all the way there was no communication there because of Serb patrols, and the Serb settlements were also a hindrance, those between Osmace and Biljeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name a couple of those settlements? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Postolje, Podrid are the Serb villages, and the patrols from Bozici and Blazevici cut the communication in half and on the other side, Mljecva, Obarak, Zaviganj. All the names I mentioned are the Serb villages. They communicated this between themselves but they interrupted a communication between Osmace and Biljeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Poznanovici has been marked on the map already. Again, in June 1992, which if any Serb settlements stood in the way of contacts between Osmace and Poznanovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Postolje, Podrid, Grubanovici. On the other side, towards the north, Crkvina, Mlecva, Obarak, Zaviganj, and Lijesce. So they were on both sides. There were Blazevici here, and patrols were on the left and on the right from Biljeg. And to reiterate it was a wooded area, an elevation point, and on both sides there were Serb settlements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. When we turn to Mocevici that's of course beyond Poznanovici as far as Osmace is concerned. I take it that there were the same impediments to contact with Mocevici that you had with Poznanovici, or were they different with other impediments?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: The main obstacles from Brezani and on the other side Ratkovici, Oparci, all the villages in between and their movement, of course, their patrols and convoys that were pretty regular to distribute weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, I want to ask you about Skenderovici which I think you haven't marked on the map yet, and if you could find Skenderovici and mark it? And the same question again really, what stood in the way of contacts between Osmace and Skenderovici in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Turija, Brezani, and on the other side, Ducici, Ratkovici, and there was regular communication between them, as well as Oparci. So we had no links with Skenderovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact finally, Srebrenica. Did you have, you in Osmace, did you have contacts with Srebrenica, the town of Srebrenica in June 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, was preventing you from having those contacts?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: The Serb villages en route, as well as the Serb patrols, Brezani and Turija were there, and on the other side, Srpska Jasenovo, linked to Podravanje. And looking from the road, on the right, there were Pribicevac and Spat, Brezani and Turija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in June 1992 -- yes, obviously the village names will have to be corrected afterwards in the transcript. I won't spell them all out now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is a daily occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it's certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you in June 1992 have Motorolas or RUPs, I think they're called, or any other sort of radio device, you in Osmace?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No, none. And not even in March of 1993. All the way until Osmace fell, we had no Motorolas, no communication devices in Osmace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Moving on to a slightly different area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones, Judge Eser, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Just as a matter of clarification, could the witness perhaps state once more which time he's speaking about when you had all this restrictions on communications? Which period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is the period between April, May, and June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: From April to June, you would not have --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the end of June of 1992. The entire month of June, there was no communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Eser and thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll ask if the witness can be shown Prosecution Exhibit P73. And while that's being presented, it's the Bajramovici document dated 20 May 1992. It states that it's a decision to form the Srebrenica municipal TO staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I simply want to ask you this: Firstly, do you know of a place called Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could locate it on the map and circle it, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: [Marks]. To the west of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, now on the 20th of May 1992, were you in Osmace able freely to pass to Bajramovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No, never. Until the end of 1992 one couldn't communicate with Bajramovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll see in this document a reference to Ahmo Tihic from Lijesce. Now, you've mentioned Lijesce in Skelani already in your testimony. You've also --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that one -- in fact you've said that all Muslim villages in Skelani were ethnically cleansed or people were expelled in May 1992. Would that include Lijesce?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, here, Tihic is described as, "an outstanding activist in armed resistance against the aggressor in the area of Skelani." To your knowledge, was there ever armed resistance organised by the Muslims in the Skelani area in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: In the first Serb offensive, Lijesce and Skelani were torched as well as a dozen other Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that's inaccurate information, would you say, regarding Tihic?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: It is not true. This is incorrect information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told us about Ratkovici and I take it there is no objection in me summarising the evidence which has been given so far. I can even give page and line reference if need be. You said from Ratkovici they shelled your village, Osmace, on the 8th of May 1992. You said you saw -- were aware of weapons being delivered to Ratkovici in 1992 on four or five occasions. Is that a correct summary of what you've told us?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the 21st of June 1992, were you aware of any Serb military presence in Ratkovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We supposed so because shelling was coming from that direction. That is to the east of Osmace. There were Ratkovici and Fakovici there and there was shelling non-stop. The shelling of all of the Muslim villages. In one -- they were together in one direction, both Ratkovici and Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Aside from the shelling, were you aware whether actually in the village of Ratkovici itself there was any sort of military presence or not?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: We had no information in Osmace because we had no contact. It was a village further away. We had no contact with Ratkovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of a place called Bradjevina?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I've heard of it but I don't know it. I was never there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you hear at any stage of any military action undertaken in Ratkovici or any military activity in June -- I'll lead the date. On the 21st of June 1992, were you aware of an action occurring on that date?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear at think stage that Ratkovici had fallen?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I don't know when, perhaps in October or -- I may have heard in July. I don't know exactly. Maybe in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you hear precisely?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: We heard that Ratkovici attacked the Muslim village of Poznanovici, and they torched a part of that village, and the villagers went after them to try to repel them and they came into their village, and they fled towards Fakovici. That's what we heard. I believe it was July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Two clarifications. When you say they torched a part of that village, who is "they" and which is "that village"?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: The Serbs broke into a part of a Muslim village called Poznanovici and they torched it. They killed a number of shepherds who were guarding sheep and working in the fields. And those lads from those villages, Podkorjen and Poznanovici, went after them and they entered Ratkovici. And so they fled in the direction of Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've told us when you heard about this, you think maybe in July. When did -- when you did hear about it --

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I think in -- I think it was in the beginning of July. I wasn't really interested, to be honest. I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Just to be entirely clear, are you saying that you believe the action or that these events took place at the beginning of July or that you heard of them at the beginning of July, just so that it's clear?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I heard about it in July, and I don't really know when the event took place. Since they were under attack in Poznanovici, they were shelled, in Podkorjen and Debici. As well they were being shelled on a daily basis from Mlecka, Obarak, Ratkovici, Ducici, it was all done on a daily basis. And there was a lot of shooting from infantry weapons, et cetera. All that went on on a daily basis, and at some point in the beginning of July we heard that they entered that Serb village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did you get this information that you've just given us -- from whom did you get that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Some local people. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But local from which villages, if you can remember that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Poznanovici or Podkorjen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to ask you about -- it's paragraph of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. indictment, paragraph 30 of the indictment which says, "On the 21st and 27th of June 1992, the village of Ratkovici, including the surrounding hamlets of Bradjevina, Ducici, and Gornji Ratkovici were attacked. Srebrenica TO, Osmace TO, Kragljivoda TO, Skenderovici TO, and Biljeg TO participated in this attack." So I want to ask you a couple of questions about that allegation. You've told us already that you didn't have in Osmace organised groups like a TO. Did you or any of your fighters go from Osmace to Ratkovici in late June to fight there, June 1992, to your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I can state with a great deal of responsibility that as far as my group of 20 or 50 something men from Osmace are concerned, nobody participated in any action in the area of Ratkovici, and Kragljivoda, because there was no physical activity. There was no physical contact. There was no possibility for them to get there from Kragljivoda. In Kragljivoda there were about 15 people guarding the road. The crossing there. And there was no way they could withdraw in that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'm going to move on now briefly from June 1992 into the summer, July, August, and September 1992. You've told us that you had refugees in Osmace. How many, roughly? Can you say how many refugees you had in Osmace in that period, the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1992, there might have remained between 300 and 400 people in the village because I had said in the beginning that most of them had left and gone to Slovenia, Germany, and elsewhere. Perhaps there could have been 1.200 up to 1.500 inhabitants and refugees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could just tell us briefly how -- how the situation in Osmace develop? And by the situation, I mean the humanitarian refugee and the military situation in July August, September of 1992, if you could give us a snapshot?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: In April 1992, the supply of any kind of commodities and especially foodstuffs to Srebrenica was cut off. And people withdrew into villages, and there were some supplies, some reserves, but they had been exhausted but as I've said there were 3 to 4 times more refugees at the time than the local population. So that there was a great deal of panic in the village. There was nothing to eat. The hygiene condition was -- conditions were bad. There was no freedom of movement. There was shelling every day, and people were getting killed and wounded. People were dying. The wounded were dying because there was no medical assistance whatsoever. So it was a state of hopelessness really. And people felt they were in hell, and it was a village in which originally there was a thousand people and then 300 remained and then new people came along and there was no food. Everything had been destroyed. There was total chaos in April, May, and June, in the area of Osmace. As to any combat activity, as I said it was something we experienced on a daily basis, this daily shelling, from all sides, from all Serb positions, and there was no choice. One had to do something. In all that, Brezani created most problems. It was to the west of Osmace. We were unable to work the land in the fields. We weren't able to take care of our cattle because they were shooting at us all the time, below that village, and they were using mortars as well. So from that western side, we had no way of getting out and we had to do something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned already in the course of your testimony a place called Fakovici, and again I'm summarising for the sake of the record, you've referred to a training centre in Ruljevici, which is near Fakovici. You said that weapons arrived en masse in your area from Fakovici by horse. You've stated how weapons were transported from Fakovici to Brezani by helicopter, and you've also told us that Sefik Mandzic stepped on a mine on the way to Fakovici. So there is no need to repeat that evidence. I just want to ask you firstly, if you're aware of any sort of military presence in Fakovici prior to October 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain -- describe that for us, what your information was about Fakovici prior to October 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes. We received information from the field -- I mean the villages that gravitated in that direction, we found out from them that there were large numbers of soldiers, Serb soldiers there, that they were involved in training at Fakovici and Ruljevici all the time and that they came from Skelani and Bajina Basta, and they were going in the direction of Bratunac, and that there were units from Bijeljina in that area, white -- the White Eagles and other volunteers from Serbia. And we knew that whenever any volunteers from Serbia came along, they were weekend visitors, as it were, and they used to set up ambushes when Muslim residents went back to their villages to collect food, and there was constant shelling and shooting in Podkorjen, Jagodnja, Joseva, so that was our impression of what going on down below.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there were large numbers of soldiers, Serb soldiers, there. Is that soldiers who were passing through or actually you talking about a permanent stationing of soldiers in Fakovici? What precisely are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Fakovici had a battalion of the JNA army. They were fully equipped. They might have had somewhere between 500 and 600 soldiers, so that battalion was stationed in Fakovici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you go to Fakovici in 1992?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of October, we had already been in touch with Sefik because there had been a powerful attack at -- on Kragljivoda. I think I went up there on the 4th of October and there were 20 people with me in my group, and Sefik and I went to Jagodnja, to a Muslim village called Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Can you locate Jagodnja on the map, please?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're also circling Joseva. How far are those villages from Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Seven or eight, no, five or six kilometres away but those two villages, Jagodnja and Joseva are next to one another. Those were two Muslim villages and Serbs went there on the 4th, and they killed quite a few civilians and they torched a part of the village and they captured some of the Muslim civilians and they took them away. So Jagodnja and Joseva are Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for the record, it's 4th of October 1992, correct?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 4th of October. I was at Kragljivoda. That's what I said. I was at Kragljivoda to help Sefik out on the 4th of October and in the early morning hours on the 5th of October -- no, maybe at around 8.00 in fact, we went in the direction of Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can just explain why you went in the direction of Joseva -- Jagodnja and Joseva, please?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: In the course of the morning, some civilians came along and they were fleeing Jagodnja and Joseva because they had been attacked by the Serbs from Fakovici, Voljevica, and Boljevici, and they were running away and they told us that those Muslim villages were on fire. And Sefik Mandzic, who had about 30 to 40 people with him, and I had 20 people with me because on that day, Kragljivoda had experienced a powerful attack and those so those of us who were at Osmace came out to help and he asked me if I would be willing to go with him and I accepted even though I was rather tired. And so in the morning we set out for Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, please, again it's a question of clarification and trying to follow the witness's evidence. He's given evidence that he went with 20 men -- 20 people, to see Sefik, there has been no explanation who those 20 people were or why he went to see Sefik. And you might expect that in -- if he's explaining this sojourn to that area. So I think that -- I've got my assumptions about why he went but it's not clear from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He said it. I beg to differ. If you look at, before I miss it, last line of page 84 and first line on page 83, yes, "on the 4th of October I was in Kragljivoda. That's what I said. I was at Kragljivoda to help Sefik out on the 4th of October and in the early morning -- or maybe around et cetera," so he's already stated that he went to Kragljivoda to meet Sefik to help him. MR. DI FAZIO: No problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Now the other part that you seek clarification of, namely who was those -- who were those 20, 20 persons he had with him, yes, of course, I mean perhaps Mr. Jones can address that. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Otherwise, is there anything else that you see that I can't see? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. To help him out, in what sense?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think even before he said the -- I mean -- and what I read to you was -- probably will be shorter if -- MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours I don't want to interrupt Mr. Jones's flow. Minimise it as much as possible. Perhaps I'll withdraw my objection. I'll deal with it myself later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you go to page 82, lines 9 to 13 or to 12, and "on the 5th of October we had already been in touch with Sefik because there had been a powerful attack on Kragljivoda and I think I won't up there on the 4th of October and there were 20 people with me in my group, and Sefik and I went to" - missing - "to a Muslim village called" -- and the transcript doesn't show the name. So I think that part is clear. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, it is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want further clarification on who these 20 persons -- the witness took with him were. Of course, I mean, it can be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. If I may, Your Honour, I mean, my flow is being interrupted. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not make any --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I simply want to make this point, that the evidence was clear and the comment by Mr. Di Fazio that the evidence is unclear and explanations aren't being given is in a way his comment on the unfolding evidence which I don't think is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's come to the 20 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: As far as 20 people are concerned, it's not part of my examination-in-chief. It's not my plan to elicit the names of those 20 individuals. If Mr. Di Fazio want to, he can do it in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think that that's the essence of Mr. Di Fazio's intervention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: No, I'm coming to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I gather whether these were fighters, whether they were just ordinary civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I follow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I think he means. MR. DI FAZIO: That's exactly right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please not overlap. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: That's the point I am concerned about.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I follow that equally. At the same time I'm going to explore the areas I need to explore and I think it's pretty obvious we're talking about a war, and attack, going to help someone. I don't intend to get many answers from this witness about exactly what they were doing. It's pretty obvious what they were doing. They were going to help someone who was being attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think once you have yourself made that statement, we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we all had the same assumption in any case. We were all assuming that these were not curious persons accompanying the witness to see what was happening. They were there for a purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, although I might ask this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of those 20 people who went with you, were any of them in uniform?

utterances.speaker: NESIB BURIC
utterances.text: No. They wore civilian clothes but they had arms as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we are coming to the close but I just want to deal with the part of your testimony which you've already given concerning Sefik. I think when we left off you were describing how in the early morning you proceeded and in fact, given the time, I'll deal with that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Mr. Buric, we are going to stop here for today. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. In the meantime, may I remind you again of my advice to you earlier on this morning, you're not to contact or let anyone contact you on matters related to your evidence. Yes, thank you, and I think we are sitting in this courtroom tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you.
